questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A demand treated as if it needed defending
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a demand does not need defending before it is discussed
questions.stem: On a transit planner's board a councillor writes that buses on the coastal route must run twice an hour. What does this demand need before it is argued about?

options.text: A reason the planners can answer with evidence, not a demand for automatic agreement.
It needs restating as an established fact before anyone is permitted to reply.
options.misconception: treats a demand as if it were already a settled fact

options.text: The backing of every regular rider before it may enter the board's agenda.
options.misconception: believes a demand is discussable only with unanimous support

options.text: Approval by vote before the substance of the demand can be argued at all.
options.misconception: assumes a procedural vote settles the merits of the request

questions.explanation: A demand asks for reasons and the board owes a response to the request. Calling it something that must be defended turns it into an assertion and closes off the reply the councillor actually needs.
questions.hint: Ask what the board owes the person who wrote it.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Objecting to a conclusion or to a step
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish an objection to a conclusion from an objection to a step
questions.stem: At a transit board a planner says the new express lane will cut journey times, then argues that the cost overrun means it should not be built. Explain what has gone wrong.

answer.exemplar: The planner has attacked a conclusion while the dispute turns on a step. The overrun and the journey times are separate claims, and rejecting the final answer is not the same as identifying the step that would need defending. Naming the step and showing why it fails gives the board something it can answer rather than something it must dismiss.

questions.explanation: Objections work best when aimed at the specific step that carries the conclusion. Attacking the conclusion alone leaves the supporting steps untouched and gives the board nothing concrete to weigh.
questions.hint: Point to the step, not the verdict.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: The shared premise underneath a disagreement
questions.learningObjective: Locate the shared premise holding a disagreement together

stimulus.body: Two members disagree about the evening peak timetable. One argues that the 6:10 departure must be retained because families rely on it. The other argues that the 6:10 departure must be removed because it strands staff at the depot. Both arguments assume that earlier staff shifts are already settled.

questions.stem: In the memo above, what shared premise holds the disagreement together and makes it a disagreement rather than a clash?

options.text: That the depot's shift times cannot be changed at any cost during the peak.
options.misconception: invents a fixed-shift rule nobody in the memo asserts

options.text: That the 6:10 service must go, and the first speaker is simply mistaken.
options.misconception: treats one side as the real subject of the dispute

options.text: That the earlier staff shifts are already fixed and so cannot be used as a remedy.
That family travel and depot staffing are equally valuable and must be traded off.
options.misconception: turns a factual assumption into a values weighing

questions.explanation: The memo records that earlier shifts are settled, and both speakers rely on that. Sharing that premise makes the clash a disagreement that a new consideration could settle, rather than an opposition between fixed positions.
questions.hint: Look for what the memo says both sides assume.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Concessions that strengthen a case
questions.learningObjective: Explain how conceding a weak premise strengthens an opposing case
questions.stem: A planning officer concedes that the original cost estimate was too low, then uses that concession to argue the scheme must be paused. Why does the concession strengthen the case rather than weaken it?

options.text: It shows the officer has changed position, so the pause is a fresh improvement.
options.misconception: reads a concession as evidence of intellectual progress

options.text: It removes the officer's standing to object to any later revision of the scheme.
options.misconception: confuses admitting error with losing standing altogether

options.text: It makes the case for pausing weaker, since the main point is already conceded.
options.misconception: assumes a concession always works against the person making it

options.text: It shows the original estimate was unreliable, so the case rested on that figure.

questions.explanation: A concession that the estimate was low shows the supporting figure was unsound. Once the case is known to rest on that figure, the pause is presented as a repair rather than an attack, which strengthens the officer's position.
questions.hint: Ask what the original case rested on.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Replies that keep a discussion open
questions.learningObjective: Select the reply that leaves a discussion open to further contribution
questions.stem: A member says the frequency increase on route 14 will be cancelled for budget reasons. Which reply keeps the discussion open rather than closing it?

options.text: What would have to be true about the budget for the increase to be affordable?
Why did the board vote for a budget with no room for service changes?
options.misconception: treats the reply as an accusation about the board's earlier choice

options.text: The member has already stated that the service will be cancelled.
options.misconception: just restates the claim instead of engaging with it

options.text: Most residents will be inconvenienced, so the cancellation should be reversed.
options.misconception: introduces a new argument instead of opening the existing one

questions.explanation: A reply that asks for a condition keeps the claim open to examination by everyone present. Accusations and added arguments settle the question in the speaker's favour instead of making the next move shared.
questions.hint: A good reply changes what is knowable.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: What makes a next step usable
questions.learningObjective: Choose a next step the board can actually act on
questions.stem: Which next step would make a planning discussion genuinely usable for the board meeting that follows?

options.text: Everyone files their reasoning in writing so the chair can read it aloud later.
options.misconception: delays the reply until the decision point has passed

options.text: The board names the disagreement and the facts it still needs before deciding.
The chair selects the strongest opening statement and asks the others to agree.
options.misconception: lets a speaking order settle the substance of the dispute

options.text: A planner retires the item and returns to it only if a new study is funded.
options.misconception: treats silence as a decision and defers everything

questions.explanation: A usable next step names what is disputed and what information would settle it. That gives members a shared task and keeps the disagreement attached to something that can be answered.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Claim and reply target
questions.learningObjective: Describe how a reply identifies the claim it targets
questions.stem: Two planners exchange comments about a proposed bus lane. One criticises a decision, the other defends it. Describe what each reply is aiming at and how to make the targets line up.

answer.exemplar: A reply aims at a specific claim: the thing the other person said that the reply takes to be false or unsupported. The critic here aims at the decision as stated, and the defender aims at the reasons behind it. Making the targets line up means restating the decision in a form both can point at, so the dispute is about one thing rather than two different things at once.

questions.explanation: A reply that does not say what it targets invites the other person to defend something else. Naming the claim explicitly lets both sides check whether they are talking about the same proposition.
questions.hint: Name the sentence you are answering.

questions.topic: A demand treated as if it needed defending
questions.learningObjective: Diagnose the reversal of burden in a consultation process

stimulus.body: A rider writes that the 5:40 express to the harbour should be made a permanent service. The board's response template invites the public to justify the request rather than inviting staff to explain the current service.

questions.stem: In the notice above, what is the problem with how the demand is being handled?

options.text: The comment is too brief to justify a permanent service, so it should be discarded.
options.misconception: treats brevity as a defect in the request

options.text: The rider has asked for a change the board was never entitled to consider.
options.misconception: presumes the board has no authority over the timetable

options.text: The notice should have quoted the fare policy that makes the service expensive.
options.misconception: assumes the missing detail is about cost recovery

options.text: The demand is treated as something to defend instead of something to answer.

questions.explanation: The template asks the person making the request to justify the request itself, which assumes the demand is an assertion to be disproved. A demand is a question the board owes an answer, and the template puts the burden on the wrong side.
questions.hint: Notice who is being asked to carry the burden.

questions.learningObjective: Recognise an objection aimed at a supporting step
questions.stem: A planner says the express lane will cut journey times to eighteen minutes. A councillor says eighteen minutes cannot be achieved because the junction cannot be changed. Which reply is aimed at a step rather than at the conclusion?

options.text: If the junction cannot change, the eighteen-minute estimate cannot hold.
The eighteen-minute figure must be wrong if the junction is fixed.
options.misconception: attacks the conclusion instead of the step it depends on

options.misconception: asks for clarification without engaging the claim made

options.text: The councillor's objection is aimed at a step the planner never used.
options.misconception: reframes the exchange as pointless rather than misaimed

questions.explanation: The councillor denies a condition the estimate relies on rather than rejecting the whole plan. Naming that condition shows the objection is already aimed at a step, which the planner can then defend or revise.

questions.learningObjective: Test whether two positions rest on a shared premise
questions.stem: Members split over whether to publish bus punctuality data monthly or quarterly, each assuming the other side favours openness. What shared premise would make this a real disagreement?

options.misconception: takes a method preference as a shared premise

options.text: That publishing figures will change how the service is judged by the public.
That punctuality data is measured the same way every quarter.
options.misconception: confuses a measurement question with the shared premise

options.text: That the board is free to choose either reporting rhythm at will.
options.misconception: invents a constraint nobody mentioned

questions.learningObjective: Identify the concession that helps the opposing case
questions.stem: Which concession, if made on the planning board, would strengthen the opponent's case rather than weaken it?

options.misconception: treats the conceded error as harmless to the argument

options.text: We were wrong to bring this up today, so the board may ignore us.
options.misconception: concedes the discussion itself instead of a premise

We concede the point, so the board may now close the discussion.
options.misconception: treats a concession as an invitation to stop

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Replies that keep a discussion open
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a reply that contests one link leaves a discussion open
questions.stem: A councillor says that increasing bus frequency will improve punctuality. A planner replies that punctuality depends on traffic, not on how many buses there are. Explain why the reply keeps the discussion open.

answer.exemplar: The reply challenges the link the councillor assumed between frequency and punctuality rather than refusing the topic. Because it identifies one link and leaves the rest of the argument standing, the councillor can still salvage the proposal by changing how frequency is timed, and the board can see exactly what would need to be shown before the claim could be accepted.

questions.explanation: The reply picks out one inferential step and contests it, so the rest of the argument is still available. A reply that rejects the whole proposal closes off the possibility of repair.
questions.hint: Find the link it contests.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: What makes a next step usable
questions.learningObjective: Identify the assumption a proposed deferral depends on

stimulus.body: The chair proposes that the board settle the route 14 frequency question at this meeting and defer the fare question to the next one. A member objects that the two are linked because the fare shortfall is what limits the frequency increase.

questions.stem: According to the note, what would make the chair's proposed next step work?

options.text: The board accepts that the fare question is not needed to decide the frequency question.
The chair allows the member to present the linking argument before any vote.
options.misconception: mistakes speaking time for a step that produces information

options.text: The member agrees with the deferral and asks for the item to be minuted.
options.misconception: treats agreement on process as settling the substance

options.text: The route 14 timetable is produced for the record before the meeting begins.
options.misconception: supplies a document rather than resolving the disagreement

questions.explanation: A deferral is only usable if the deferred question is genuinely not needed for the deferred decision. Without that acceptance the link stays live and the board will settle a question it has not actually decided.
questions.hint: Ask what the deferral assumes.

questions.learningObjective: Match a reply to the claim its author was answering
questions.stem: In a debate about shuttle frequency, one speaker defends a two-year pilot and another attacks the pilot as a way of avoiding a decision. Which reply targets the right claim?

options.misconception: answers a cost claim the critic never actually made

options.text: The pilot gathers evidence before commitment, which is the claim the critic denies.
Two years is enough to judge the service, so the critic is being unfair.

options.misconception: attacks the critic's motives instead of the claim made

options.misconception: demands support the request has not asked for

options.misconception: leans on a general truth rather than this argument

options.text: That the timetable should have been designed in the first place.
options.misconception: criticises the past rather than the reasoning given

options.text: That drivers will indeed refuse, so the member is right about the outcome.
options.misconception: agrees with the conclusion instead of testing the reasoning

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: The shared premise underneath a disagreement
questions.learningObjective: Explain how surfacing a shared premise changes the disagreement
questions.stem: Two planners disagree about whether a proposed fare rise is affordable. Explain how identifying a shared premise could change what the discussion is about.

answer.exemplar: If both planners assume that affordability is judged against average household income, then the disagreement is not about whether the rise is fair but about what comparison to use. Naming that shared premise lets them test it, and if it turns out to be contestable, the disagreement may dissolve or shift onto new ground rather than staying locked on opposite verdicts.

questions.explanation: A shared premise gives the disagreement a shape that can be inspected. Once it is named, the members can agree on the criterion, or discover that they never agreed on it at all.
questions.hint: Look below the two verdicts.

options.misconception: reads a conceded survey as a licence to silence

options.text: It shows the case against the extension rested on a poorly sampled survey.
It shows that the planner has changed her mind about the extension.
options.misconception: mistakes a conceded method for a changed conclusion

options.text: It leaves the extension exactly as contestable as it was before.

questions.topic: Replies that keep a discussion open
questions.learningObjective: Explain why adding an option does not close a disagreement
questions.stem: A member suggests the board ask the regional authority for funds rather than cut the timetable. Why is this a reply that keeps the discussion open?

options.text: It offers a third option, so the original two are no longer in dispute.
options.misconception: assumes adding an option settles the existing disagreement

options.text: It shifts responsibility, so the board avoids deciding anything at all.

It gives the board time, so no decision is needed at this meeting.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A demand treated as if it needed defending
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish a demand from a claim and the burdens each carries
questions.stem: A business group demands that the airport express be given priority at the airport end. Explain how this demand differs from a claim the board could simply accept or reject.

answer.exemplar: The request asks the board to do something, and the board's task is to give reasons for its answer rather than to prove the request false. That shifts the burden onto the board to explain its decision, whereas a claim must be supported by whoever advances it. The demand still has content that can be argued, but it is not itself something that has to be defended before discussion can begin.

questions.explanation: A demand invites an answer with reasons; a claim must arrive already supported. Calling the demand something that needs defending reverses who carries the burden of explanation.
questions.hint: Ask who owes the reasons.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: What makes a next step usable
questions.learningObjective: Judge whether an intermediate step is worth taking
questions.stem: A board has three months before a depot decision. Describe what would make an intermediate step worth taking rather than merely filling time.

answer.exemplar: An intermediate step earns its place when it settles something the decision depends on, or when it produces information that changes what the members can choose. Agreeing the survey method and publishing the results would be worth the time; agreeing to revisit the item in a further three months adds nothing to what the board knows, and only delays the choice it has to make.

questions.explanation: A step is worth taking when it changes the board's knowledge or its options. Steps that only defer a decision consume time without producing anything the members can use.
questions.hint: Ask what the step produces.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Claim and reply target
questions.learningObjective: Recognise the reply that names and then disputes its target
questions.stem: In an exchange about who should fund a new bus route, which reply is aimed at the claim it was answering?

options.text: Funding is a complicated matter that nobody has properly examined.
options.misconception: replaces the reply with a general remark about the topic

options.text: The route should be funded locally because the region has other priorities.
options.misconception: answers a different question about what the region should fund

options.text: Yes, and the region has agreed to cover it in the past as well.
options.misconception: concedes the claim and adds an irrelevant precedent

options.text: The claim was that funding falls to the region, and the reply disputes that.

questions.explanation: A reply that names its target and then disputes it engages the proposition that was actually put. The alternatives either shift the ground, generalise, or concede the point without argument.
questions.hint: Say the claim, then answer it.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: A demand treated as if it needed defending
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a demand is answered rather than refuted
questions.stem: A passenger group demands that the late bus on route 22 be reinstated. Explain how this demand should be handled differently from a claim that the same service was unfair.

answer.exemplar: The group has asked for something, so the board owes a reply with reasons, whereas a claim about unfairness would have required the group to support it. The board must therefore set out why the service was withdrawn and what would have to change for it to return, rather than inviting the group to prove the route was unfair. Treating the demand as a claim lets the board avoid the reasons the request is owed.

questions.explanation: A demand calls for the board's reasons, while a claim calls for the claimant's support. Handling the request as a claim leaves the group without the answer it asked for.
questions.hint: Ask who carries the burden here.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Objecting to a conclusion or to a step
questions.learningObjective: Find the step that a loaded statistic depends on

stimulus.body: Note: the controller proposes that the 7:05 service be removed because two vehicles are off the road. A councillor objects that removing the service would push passengers onto the 6:40, which is already full on school days.

questions.stem: In the note above, which reply is best aimed at a step rather than at the conclusion?

options.text: The 6:40 is the only alternative, so the 7:05 removal must be reversed.
options.misconception: goes straight to the outcome instead of the reasoning

options.text: Are school day and non-school day travel being counted together?
Two vehicles are off the road, so no proposal is possible this month.
options.misconception: generalises a vehicle shortage into a ban on any proposal

options.text: The controller should be asked to model the two options before either is chosen.
options.misconception: calls for more work rather than naming the step at issue

questions.explanation: The objection rests on the 6:40 being full, and that may depend on whether school days are counted with other days. Separating the two counts tests the step the conclusion depends on instead of jumping to the outcome.
questions.hint: Ask what the fullness figure includes.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: The shared premise underneath a disagreement
questions.learningObjective: Locate a disagreement one level below where it is argued
questions.stem: One member says the station should be staffed and another says it should not. Both assume passengers can reach the platform without help. What does this shared assumption make their disagreement?

options.text: It means the disagreement is not about staffing at all.
options.misconception: concludes that a shared premise dissolves the dispute outright

options.text: It means the disagreement is about staffing and can be settled by staffing evidence.
options.misconception: assumes the shared premise settles the question it supports

options.text: It means the disagreement is about accessibility, and the staffing views follow from it.
It means the disagreement is settled because both members agree on it.
options.misconception: confuses sharing a premise with sharing a conclusion

questions.explanation: Both views about staffing follow from a shared assumption about accessibility, so the dispute is really located one level below where it is being argued. Settling the accessibility question would dissolve the staffing disagreement rather than decide it.
questions.hint: Ask what the staffing views rest on.

questions.subject: SEMINAR
questions.topic: Concessions that strengthen a case
questions.learningObjective: Explain how conceding an input limits the support available
questions.stem: An officer concedes that the modelling used last year's fuel price, then argues the scheme should still go ahead. Why would that concession matter to the board?

options.text: It shows the fuel price is no longer relevant to the decision.
options.misconception: dismisses the input rather than explaining what it was for

options.text: It shows the officer's modelling cannot be relied on at all.
options.misconception: treats one dated input as discrediting the whole exercise

options.text: It shows the board should commission fresh modelling before deciding anything.
options.misconception: turns a concession into a demand for a new study

options.text: It narrows the grounds the officer can stand on, since the figure rests on that price.

questions.explanation: Conceding which input was used tells the board what the estimate rested on, and it narrows the support the officer can draw on. The board can then judge whether other reasons survive that input.
questions.hint: Ask what the estimate was resting on.
